claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys exhibit enhanced structural stability at elevated temperatures.
Increased configurational entropy causes the enhanced structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Increased configurational entropy mitigates phase separation at elevated temperatures.
The high-entropy nanoalloys begin as homogeneous solid solutions containing multiple principal elements.
Configurational entropy and atomic disorder are the structural mediators governing stability.
Increased configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution phase.
Increased configurational entropy reduces high-temperature segregation.
High-entropy nanoalloys containing more principal elements will undergo less structural degradation than alloys containing fewer principal elements under identical high-temperature exposure.
Nanoalloys with more principal elements will exhibit less grain growth than those with fewer principal elements.
Nanoalloys with more principal elements will exhibit less phase separation than those with fewer principal elements.
The prediction may not apply to conventional alloys or alloys with fewer principal elements.
The relationship between the number of principal elements and the degree of high-temperature structural stability is not fully characterized.
A comparison at approximately 800°C for approximately 100 hours can test the predicted stability trend.
Greater structural degradation in high-entropy nanoalloys than in standard alloys, or absence of the predicted trend with principal-element count, would falsify the hypothesis.
